source.title: JALMBench: Benchmarking Jailbreak Vulnerabilities in Audio Language Models
source.authors: Zi-Fan Peng; Yule Liu; Zhen Sun; Mingchen Li; Zeren Luo; Jing-Yi Zheng; Wenhan Dong; Xin-Lei He; Xue-Chao Wang; Ying-Jie Xue; Shengmin Xu; Xin-Yi Huang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports audio-language-model jailbreak rates, but does not test few-example fine-tuning, benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-opening prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, localized safety parameters, or training to deepen safety. Its tested attack mechanisms are different from the specific mechanisms in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported ASRs for the paper's prompt and audio attacks are relevant to general jailbreak vulnerability, but do not test the mechanisms named by V1–V7. They are recorded under fits_no_version. Background statements and results attributed to cited work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks jailbreak attacks on 12 audio-language models: persuasion, DAN and DeepInception templates, in-context harmful demos, audio edits, SSJ spelling, and AdvWave. None of these are harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefilled compliant openings, suffix or decoding attacks aimed at the response opening, parameter localization, or deepening training. Qi et al. (arXiv:2310.03693) is cited only as the source of the LLM-judge scoring rubric. The ASRs show general jailbreak vulnerability, not the shallow-alignment mechanisms.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also say text-based alignment partially transfers to audio, that discrete or interleaved audio-text architectures generalize safety better, and that existing prompt- and response-level defenses help only modestly (best cuts about 18–20 points), with a utility trade-off for prompt defenses.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks a range of text-transferred and audio-originated jailbreaks; it does not apply the fine-tuning or token-position methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ASR varies by attack type, input modality, model, and architecture. The authors also report substantially greater variation across languages than across speaker gender, accents, TTS systems, and human voices.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 12 LALMs, average ASR was 45.4% for SSJ, 54.2% for AMSE, 88.9% for BoN and 96.2% for black-box AdvWave. Text-transferred attacks reached up to 86.3% (text) and 90.4% (audio) with PAP (Tables 8–9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Audio-language models' safety alignment is broadly vulnerable to text-transferred and audio-originated jailbreaks, with optimized and best-of-N audio attacks near ceiling.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla harmful-query ASR averaged 17.0% for text and 21.5% for audio. Some models showed large gaps, e.g. LLaMA-Omni at 9.6% text versus 58.9% audio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-based safety alignment transfers only partially to the audio modality of LALMs, depending on architecture.

record.problems: The paper uses an LLM judge for ASR, although it reports reliability checks including human verification. ASR uncertainty intervals are not stated. The authors note that some attack datasets, such as DAN, have limited audio samples.
record.rows_left_out: The individual model-by-attack cells in Tables 8–10, defense-specific outcomes in Tables 2 and 12, and other voice-diversity results were not extracted; the rows here retain aggregate results relevant to general jailbreak vulnerability, which do not test V1–V7.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples. ICA uses in-context demos, not weight updates.
No per-token KL or position-wise comparison of aligned and base models.

No prefilling of compliant openings, no suffix attacks on text tokens, and no decoding changes; greedy decoding is used throughout. AdvWave white-box optimizes audio perturbations, but the paper does not analyse response-opening tokens.
No weight or rank localization analysis. t-SNE of final hidden states concerns modality separation, not localization.
No analysis of whether data or objective causes shallowness. The paper attributes audio vulnerability to modality integration and architecture.
No training that deepens alignment. Defenses are system prompts and output filters.

missing.what: White-box AdvWave ASR averaged 81.2% on LLaMA-Omni, Qwen2-Audio and SpeechGPT. This is gradient-optimized audio, the nearest analogue to suffix optimization, but it is not linked to response-opening tokens.
missing.versions: none (closest to V4, not a test of it)

missing.what: Qualitative note that Gemini-2.0 and SALMONN often reply 'Sure' without substantive harmful follow-up.

record.verdict_notes: Row values match Tables 8–9. Table 2 appears to swap the ICA and DAN column labels relative to Table 8 (42.3 vs 22.8); the rows follow Table 8. Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the only citation of an original source is the Qi et al. judge rubric, and shallow alignment is not discussed. The text includes an attack-refinement prompt with instructions; it was treated as data.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilling compliant response tokens, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, and whether bypassing early response tokens causes compliance.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training safety beyond initial response tokens and testing its durability.
